title: The Ostrich Effect: Why You Stop Checking Your Money When It Hurts
hook_text: LOGINS FALL 9.5% AFTER A MARKET DROP

beats.say: Investors log in nine and a half percent less after a market drop. You might too.
beats.visual: extreme macro of one fat dewdrop sliding off a fern frond edge, a whole stormy sky flipped upside down inside it

beats.say: Economists call this the ostrich effect: avoiding bad news by simply not looking.
beats.visual: low angle macro of a small beetle with its head pushed deep into a moss crevice, razor focus on its glossy back

beats.say: Karlsson, Loewenstein and Seppi published the paper on it in two thousand nine.
beats.visual: overhead flat-lay of a split seed pod on dark soil with three seeds spilled out, soft side light

beats.say: Later, a Vanguard study tracked one point one million investors over two years.
beats.visual: extreme wide aerial of a hillside meadow of thousands of identical tiny blue flax flowers, a sea of blue specks

beats.say: They reviewed over eight hundred fifty million daily logins and trades.
beats.visual: macro along an unbroken trail of ants carrying crumbs across rough bark, focus sweeping down the line

beats.say: After the prior day's stock market fell, logins dropped nine and a half percent.
beats.visual: backlit macro of a spider web strung with dew where several strands sag empty and bare, glowing green bokeh behind

beats.say: In everyday life, it is the retirement app you skip and the statement left sealed.
beats.visual: eye level macro of a tightly shut pine cone resting in damp moss, scales clamped closed, drizzle beads on it

beats.say: Here is the part nobody tells you. Investors holding only bonds did the opposite, logging in more when stocks fell.
beats.visual: side view macro of two snails creeping in opposite directions along one wet branch, antennae lifted, silver trails

beats.say: The honest catch: these are averages from one provider, and logging in less does not prove anyone lost money.
beats.visual: overhead macro of a dry mud flat cracked into narrow plates, one thin crack widening toward the camera

beats.say: The counter move: pick a review date, like once a quarter, and open your accounts then, whatever the market did.
beats.visual: low sun casts the long shadow of one grass blade across a pale river stone, macro from ground level

beats.say: Write down one question for each review, like whether your savings rate and mix still fit your plan.
beats.visual: backlit low angle macro of a clover seedling with two small leaves pushing up through brown leaf litter

beats.say: This is education, not advice. Looking on a schedule is easier than looking on a mood.
beats.visual: long lens view of a still pond at dawn with one lily pad, drifting mist and reeds reflected in the water

beats.say: Follow for the money rules school never taught you.
beats.visual: silhouette macro of a single dandelion seed drifting upward through soft green bokeh against low gold sun

description: In a Review of Financial Studies paper using Vanguard data on 1.1 million investors over two years, account logins fell 9.5 percent after a decline in the previous day's stock market. Economists call avoiding bad financial news the ostrich effect. A fixed review date is one way to look anyway. Educational only, not financial advice.
first_comment: Do you open your accounts when the market is down, or wait until it feels safe? Educational only, not financial advice.

facts.claim: Account logins fell by 9.5% after market declines (a decline in the previous day's stock market); the data covered over 852 million day-to-day observations on logins and trades for 1.1 million Vanguard investors over two years
facts.basis: Sicherman, Loewenstein, Seppi and Utkus (2016), Financial Attention, Review of Financial Studies 29(4): 863-897; Carnegie Mellon University news release, December 2015

facts.claim: The 'ostrich effect' on selective attention to financial information was published in 2009
facts.basis: Karlsson, Loewenstein and Seppi (2009), The ostrich effect: Selective attention to information, Journal of Risk and Uncertainty 38(2): 95-115

facts.claim: Investors holding only bonds showed the reverse pattern and were much more likely to log in when the stock market was down
facts.basis: Carnegie Mellon University news release, December 2015, on Sicherman, Loewenstein, Seppi and Utkus (2016)

facts.claim: Results are averages for one provider's investors over two years and do not predict any single person's behavior or outcomes

look: extreme macro nature photography, dew, insects, moss and seeds, razor-thin focus, soft green and gold bokeh
caption: Investors in a Vanguard study logged in 9.5% less after a market drop, a habit called the ostrich effect. These are averages, not a rule for you. A set review date is one way to keep looking. Educational content, not financial advice.
